$comment: Copilot Studio feature catalog. Drives the Lab Builder wizard. Each selected feature becomes one lab chapter. learnQueries feed the Microsoft Learn MCP server; docUrls are the pages the step deriver reads for each module, and the citation fallback when a search returns nothing relevant. steps are the fallback walk-through, used whenever no procedure on those pages matches the module closely enough, which is a common path rather than a rare one. Every feature has a level (100 Beginner: make an agent and test it; 200 Intermediate: add tools, skills, MCP servers, and workflows; 300 Advanced: custom connectors, ALM, governance, and enterprise integration) and a harness list naming the Copilot Studio harnesses (see the top-level harnesses list) whose steps and checks it describes. Optional availability (ga, preview, or retired) is set only when a Learn page states it, and optional harnessNote records a documented difference between the harnesses, sourced from the harness comparison on the harnesses-overview page. Every feature records lastVerified, the YYYY-MM-DD day someone last compared its steps, concepts, and checks against the live documentation, and verifiedAgainst, the page they compared against: one of its docUrls, or one of its thirdPartySources urls when the steps follow a vendor's own documentation. validateCatalog() requires both, generated labs quote them to learners, and the monthly accuracy audit flags any feature verified more than 180 days ago. Only change lastVerified after actually re-reading verifiedAgainst and correcting whatever drifted, because a wrong freshness date is worse than none; the procedure is in docs/lab-builder.md, 'Extending the catalog'. There is deliberately no catalog-wide review date: features are re-verified one at a time. thirdPartySources (optional, per feature) are documentation published outside Microsoft Learn — a specification or vendor reference the feature is built on — each with a vendor, a descriptive title (it becomes the link text), an https url, and a stability note saying how likely the page is to change or move. The builder reads them directly rather than through the Learn MCP server, cites them in a Vendor documentation block beside the Microsoft Learn references, and may quote one line from them. vendorHosts is the allowlist for that: the only hosts the builder will contact, matched exactly, with the reason each is trusted. Every thirdPartySources url must be on it, and every entry on it must be used by a feature, so the list never grows wider than the catalog needs. Redirects are re-checked against it on every hop.

features.name: Create an agent
features.summary: Create a new Copilot Studio agent from a natural-language description or the blank agent option.
features.whyItMatters: Everything else in Copilot Studio hangs off the agent object. Describing the agent in natural language lets Copilot Studio generate the starting name, description, instructions, and suggestions, which is the fastest path from idea to working prototype.
concepts: Agents are environment-scoped: the environment you pick decides which connectors, Dataverse tables, and DLP policies apply.
The natural-language creation flow generates a starting name, description, and instructions, and might suggest triggers, channels, knowledge sources, and tools.
You can start from a blank agent on Home or Agents if natural-language creation is unavailable or you want full control.
steps: Sign in to Copilot Studio.
Turn off **New experience** and select **Submit** to dismiss the **Feedback** panel so the **Home** page appears.
Switch to the environment you want, and optionally change the primary language, solution, and schema name.
On the **Home** page or the **Agents** page, enter a brief description of what you want your agent to do.
Review the suggestions, wait for provisioning, and configure the agent's basic features on the **Overview** page.
Test your agent and improve it.
validation: The agent appears on the **Agents** page in your lab environment.
The **Overview** page shows a name, description, and non-empty instructions.

instructions: Open the **Home** page or **Agents** page where the natural-language description box is visible.

features.name: Agent instructions & persona
features.summary: Write the instructions that define the agent's role, scope, resource-use guidance, tone, and guardrails.
features.whyItMatters: Instructions are the central directions an agent follows when it chooses resources, fills inputs, and generates responses. Vague instructions produce vague agents; explicit scope, configured-resource guidance, and escalation rules make an agent safer to hand to real users.
concepts: Instructions help the agent decide which configured tools, knowledge, topics, or other agents to call, fill inputs, and generate a response.
An agent can't follow instructions for a resource it doesn't have; configure the tools, agents, knowledge sources, and topics before referencing them.
Keep instructions simple and test changes incrementally; don't try to override citation behavior in instructions.
steps: On the **Overview** page for the agent, find **Instructions** and select **Edit**.
Add or change plain-text instructions, typing a slash when you need to reference a configured resource such as a tool, topic, agent, variable, or Power Fx expression.
State the agent's role, audience, supported tasks, and when to use named configured resources.
Add guardrails for out-of-scope requests, missing inputs, and the expected response format.
Test the changes by using the test pane or trigger test payloads.
If the agent is already published, select **Publish** to update the published version.
validation: Asking an in-scope question returns an answer that uses the configured resources as instructed.
Asking an out-of-scope question follows the documented guardrail or escalation path instead of guessing.

features.name: Generative orchestration
features.harnessNote: The Microsoft Copilot harness uses its own orchestration for every agent, so the orchestration setting described here exists only on the standard harness.
features.summary: Confirm or turn on generative orchestration so the agent can plan across topics, knowledge, tools, and other agents.
features.whyItMatters: Classic orchestration selects a topic by matching trigger phrases. Generative orchestration can select one or more topics, tools, knowledge sources, or other agents, which is what makes multi-step business questions answerable.
concepts: New agents use generative orchestration by default unless a prebuilt agent or environment admin setting changes that behavior.
The descriptions of topics, tools, agents, and knowledge sources are the most important routing signal for the orchestrator.
The activity map in the test pane shows the resources the orchestrator selected, which is your primary debugging tool.
steps: Go to the agent's **Settings** page.
In **Generative AI** under **Orchestration**, set **Use generative AI orchestration for your agent's responses?** to **Yes**.
Ask a multi-intent question that should use more than one tool, topic, agent, or knowledge source.
Open the activity map in the test pane and review which resources were selected and in what sequence.
Rewrite overlapping or vague resource descriptions, then start a fresh test and try again.
validation: The orchestration setting shows **Yes** for generative orchestration.
The activity map shows the expected resources selected in the expected order.

instructions: Open **Settings** and the **Generative AI** section.
Show the orchestration selection.

Expand the activity map so the selected resources are visible.

features.name: Model selection
features.summary: Choose the primary AI model for the agent and compare quality, latency, reasoning, and cost tradeoffs.
features.whyItMatters: Model choice is a per-agent lever on response quality, latency, and cost. Deep models fit multistep reasoning and tool-rich workflows, while general models fit faster everyday grounded answers.
concepts: Model use categories describe the workload fit: general models emphasize speed and lower cost, auto models adapt per turn, and deep models emphasize multistep reasoning.
The default model is usually the best performing generally available model and can act as a fallback if a selected model becomes unavailable.
Experimental and preview models are for evaluation, not production, and might have availability, quality, latency, billing, or data-boundary implications.
steps: Go to the agent's **Overview** page.
In the **Model** section, select the agent's primary model.
Review the available model tags and release status before choosing a model for the workload.
Choose a model whose category fits the scenario, then compare representative prompts for answer quality and latency.
Re-run your evaluation set and record the decision before publishing the agent.
validation: The **Model** section displays the selected primary model.
Representative prompts still meet the quality bar after the model change.
Any preview or experimental model choice is documented with its production and data-boundary risks.

instructions: Show the **Model** section on the agent's **Overview** page.

features.harnessNote: The Microsoft Copilot harness has its own publish flow; see mc-publish-agent.
features.summary: Publish the agent so channel users receive the latest authored content.
features.whyItMatters: Authoring changes are invisible to published channels until you publish. Even after publishing, some persistent conversations need a new session before the latest content appears.
concepts: Publishing applies the current authoring state to all channels associated with the agent.
The test chat uses the latest authoring state, while published channels use the latest published state.
In persistent channels such as Teams, entering `start over` starts a new session that can use the latest published content.

For private Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot testing, select **Open the agent in Teams**; for unauthenticated or manual-auth website testing, use the **Demo website** link.
After testing privately, select **Make the agent available to others** when you're ready to broaden access.

features.name: Test your agent
features.harnessNote: The Microsoft Copilot harness uses a Preview tab instead of this panel; see mc-preview-test.
features.summary: Use the Test your agent panel to walk through a conversation, follow the topics and nodes that fire, and watch variable values.
features.whyItMatters: Testing in the panel catches broken topics and bad variable values before users see them, and it is the quickest way to confirm what a change did.
concepts: The Test your agent panel runs a conversation as a user would, so you can check that topics trigger and the conversation flows as you expect.
Selecting a response in the test chat takes you to the topic and node that sent it; nodes that fired show a colored checkmark and border.

The panel is for design-time validation and doesn't fully replicate published channel behavior. Timer-based and background-triggered events, such as inactivity triggers, might not fire there, so test them on a published channel such as Microsoft Teams.
steps: Open your agent in Copilot Studio. If the **Test your agent** panel is hidden, select **Test** at the top of any page.
In the field at the bottom of the panel, enter a message. If the text is similar to a trigger phrase for a topic, that topic begins.
Select the agent response in the test chat to open the topic and the node that sent the response.
Select the three dots (**…**) at the top of the test panel and turn on **Track between topics** to follow the conversation automatically as it moves from topic to topic.
Select **Variables** on the secondary toolbar, switch to the **Test** tab, and expand a variable category to watch values change as the conversation continues.
After you change and save a topic, select the **Reset** icon at the top of the test panel to start a fresh conversation.
validation: A test conversation produces agent responses in the **Test your agent** panel.
Selecting a response opens the topic and node that sent it.
The **Variables** panel **Test** tab shows values for the variables used in the conversation.

features.name: Choose a harness: standard or Microsoft Copilot
features.summary: Compare the standard and Microsoft Copilot harnesses, pick one for a scenario, and learn how to reach each in Copilot Studio.
features.whyItMatters: The harness you build on decides the features, channels, and billing model of the agent, and an agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness cannot be moved back to the standard harness. Choosing deliberately avoids rework and surprise credit use.
concepts: A harness is the runtime between the model and the agent's configuration: it decides when to call the model, what to send it, how to read the result, and which tools to call. The harness affects billing, features, and capabilities.

The standard harness fits rule-based agents and structured, repeatable conversations. The Microsoft Copilot harness fits reasoning-heavy, longer-running work, such as multi-step business processes, and it uses Copilot Credits.

You choose the harness when you create an agent. An agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness can't be transferred to the standard harness, but Copilot Studio can create a Microsoft Copilot harness agent from a standard harness agent.

Learn also describes a Customer Conversation harness and a Copilot chat harness. They use separate creation paths and are outside this catalog, which covers the standard and Microsoft Copilot harnesses.
steps: Write down the scenario you want to build and whether it is short and rule-based (for example, an HR intake and routing bot) or long-running, multi-step, and file-heavy (for example, accounts payable reconciliation).
Open the **Harnesses in Copilot Studio** article and compare your scenario with the **Standard harness** and **Microsoft Copilot harness** columns of its comparison table.
Sign in to Copilot Studio and open the **Home** page.

To reach standard harness agents, select the three dots (**…**) at the bottom of the side bar, and then select **Open classic experience**. The classic experience applies to your current session only.
To create a new standard harness agent or agent flow, select **Other ways to build** on the **Home** page. You can also open an existing agent or flow from **Agents** or **Workflows**.
Record your decision, and for the Microsoft Copilot harness note the expected Copilot Credit use.
validation: You can state which harness fits the scenario and give two reasons from the comparison table.
You can reach both the new **Home** page and the classic experience.

features.name: Create an agent (Microsoft Copilot harness)
features.summary: Create an agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness, name it, write its instructions, and save it on the Build tab.
features.whyItMatters: Everything else on the Microsoft Copilot harness, including knowledge, tools, skills, and memory, hangs off this agent. Writing clear instructions up front is the main way you steer how it reasons.
concepts: Agents on the Microsoft Copilot harness use natural-language instructions, knowledge, tools, and other components to reason over context and take action. Using, building, testing, and evaluating them might consume Copilot Credits.
The last agent name you enter before the first save sets the agent's schema name, and that system name becomes read-only afterward.
The Build tab brings instructions, knowledge, tools, skills, connected agents, the model, and memory into one place. The Preview, Evaluate, and Monitor tabs cover testing and operating the agent.
steps: Sign in to Copilot Studio.

On the **Home** page, select the **Agent** tile. Alternatively, select **Agents** in the side pane and then **New agent**. The agent opens in the designer on the **Build** tab with the name field in focus.
Enter a name for your agent in the name field.
Optionally, use the **Agent settings** panel to change the primary language, solution, and schema name before you save.
In the **Instructions** section, describe how the agent should behave, including its role, tone, and any rules it must follow.
Select the **Save** icon. If you skipped the name, enter it when prompted and select **Save**.
On the **Build** tab, confirm that the agent now offers knowledge, tools, skills, connected agents, model, and memory as components you can add next.
validation: The agent appears on the **Agents** page in your lab environment.

features.name: Publish an agent (Microsoft Copilot harness)
features.summary: Publish the agent to its channels, check readiness and data-policy blocks, and republish after changes.
features.whyItMatters: Changes on the Build tab reach users only after you publish, and data policies can block channels. Knowing the publish flow and its failure messages prevents a launch day surprise.
concepts: Publishing needs a saved name, description, and instructions, and Learn recommends you test in the Preview pane first. If something is missing, the publish dialog tells you what to complete.
Your organization's data policies can block channels or connectors, which disables them in the publish flow. The built-in test channel that powers Preview does not block publishing on its own.

The Microsoft Copilot harness supports fewer publishing channels than the standard harness. Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams, the demo website, and web app embedding are available, and an agent with triggers needs an extra activation step after publishing.
steps: Open your agent in Copilot Studio and select **Publish**.
In the **Publish agent** dialog, review the agent details and select and configure each channel you want to publish to.
If the dialog says the agent is missing a name, description, or instructions, complete them before you continue.
Select **Publish** to confirm, and wait for the dialog to show that publishing finished.
When publishing succeeds, use the confirmation to share the agent or add it to the organization catalog.

After you change the agent on the **Build** tab, select **Publish** in the upper-right corner, review the **Publish your changes** dialog, and select **Publish** to confirm. If publishing fails, select **Retry**.
validation: The **Publish agent** dialog reports a successful publish.
The channels you selected are configured and none are blocked by a data policy.

features.name: Upgrade a standard agent to the Microsoft Copilot harness
features.summary: Ask Copilot Studio to upgrade a standard harness agent, then review what was migrated and rebuild what was not.
features.whyItMatters: Migration is re-architecture, not a mechanical copy. Reading the upgrade report tells you which knowledge, topic logic, and child agents you must rebuild before the new agent matches the old one.
concepts: The upgrade creates a copy of the agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness. It carries over instructions, tools, and suggested prompts, and the upgrade consumes credits.

Custom topics can be rebuilt as skills or workflows. Knowledge sources, Power Fx expressions, and child agents aren't migrated, and Azure AI Search grounding must be reconfigured through Foundry IQ or an Azure AI Search connector tool.
Learn recommends migrating only for a scenario-level benefit. A working standard harness agent doesn't need to move, and standard harness agents keep running.
steps: On the Copilot Studio **Home** page, enter a request such as "upgrade my Coffee Coach agent" in the input box, using the name of your own standard harness agent.
Follow the progress in the chat, and confirm or clarify details when Copilot Studio asks, for example whether it found the right agent.
When it finishes, find the new agent card, which shows the agent name followed by **(Upgraded)**, and any workflow cards.
Select the **Open** icon on a card to view or customize the artifact.
Review the report of what was migrated, what needs attention, and what was skipped.
Re-add knowledge sources, rebuild Power Fx logic and child-agent behavior, and test the core journeys on the **Preview** tab.
validation: A new agent labeled **(Upgraded)** exists alongside the original standard harness agent.
You have a list of skipped items, such as knowledge sources, and a plan to rebuild each one.

features.name: Topics & trigger phrases
features.harnessNote: The Microsoft Copilot harness has no topics: hooks run workflows at lifecycle events instead, and custom topics can be rebuilt as skills or workflows. See mc-hooks and mc-upgrade-from-standard.
features.summary: Create custom topics with trigger phrases and descriptions, and understand the system topics every agent starts with.
features.whyItMatters: Topics define deterministic conversation paths for scenarios that need an exact script, such as disclosures, intake forms, and escalation. System topics handle common events, so reviewing them prevents custom topics from accidentally duplicating built-in behavior.
concepts: Agents can use generative orchestration or classic orchestration to choose how to respond; in generative orchestration, topic descriptions help the agent choose the topic.
Classic orchestration uses trigger phrases as examples; customer input does not need to exactly match a phrase to trigger the topic.

System topics such as Conversation Start, Conversational boosting, Escalate, Fallback, Multiple Topics Matched, On Error, Reset Conversation, and Sign in are built in; you can customize or turn off what you do not need.
steps: Go to the **Topics** page for your agent and close the test panel for better visibility.
Select **Add a topic**, and then select **From blank**.
On the **Trigger** node, select **…** > **Properties**.
In **On Recognized Intent properties**, select **Phrases**, then enter 5 to 10 varied trigger phrases under **Add phrases**.
Select **Details** and enter a topic name, optional display name, and **Description**.
Select **Save**, then test the topic with a phrase you did not train on.
validation: The topic is listed on the **Topics** page after you save it.
The topic triggers from an untrained but semantically similar phrase.
System topics still handle conversation start, fallback, and escalation events.

features.name: Entities & variables
features.harnessNote: Custom entities are not supported on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
features.summary: Create custom entities, collect values in Question nodes, and reuse the resulting variables across topics.
features.whyItMatters: Entities turn free text into structured values your tools can use, and variables keep those values available to the parts of the conversation that need them. Without this structure, topics have to ask for the same information repeatedly.
concepts: Prebuilt entities cover common information types such as money, numbers, names, dates, and cities.
Closed list entities work best for manageable domain lists with synonyms; regular expression entities work for patterned identifiers.
Question nodes automatically create output variables; pass variables between topics or convert to global variables only when the value must outlive one topic.
steps: Open **Settings** > **Entities**, then select **Add an entity** > **New entity**.
Choose **Closed list** or regular expression, enter values under **List items**, add **Synonyms** where useful, and select **Save**.
Open the topic from **Topics**, select **Add node**, and then select **Ask a question**.
Under **Identify**, select a prebuilt or custom entity, and rename the output variable in **Variable properties**.
Use **Variables** to pass or return values between topics, or convert the variable to a global variable when multiple topics need it.
Test with natural sentences and synonyms, and watch the variable value in the **Variables** panel.
validation: The selected prebuilt entity extracts the value from a natural sentence, not just a bare answer.
The custom entity recognizes at least one synonym you defined.
A receiving topic uses the passed value without asking the user the same question again.

features.name: Adaptive Cards & rich responses
features.summary: Add display or interactive Adaptive Cards and use Power Fx when a card needs values from variables.
features.whyItMatters: A wall of prose is hard to use on a phone or in Teams. Adaptive Cards let you show key values, status, and actions in a layout users can scan quickly.
concepts: Use a **Message** node or **Question** node for noninteractive cards, and use an **Adaptive Card** node when the user must submit a response.
Copilot Studio supports Adaptive Cards schema version 1.6 and earlier, but the target channel can limit the version that actually renders.
Use JSON for static card structure and **Formula** in the card properties when the card needs dynamic topic or agent variables.

Select **Save**, confirm the preview appears, and test the card in your target channel.

features.name: Power Fx in topics
features.summary: Use Power Fx formulas to set variables and evaluate conditions inside topic logic.
features.whyItMatters: Power Fx is the formula layer for exact transformations, mappings, and date or text logic inside a topic. When a value has to be deterministic, compute it instead of asking the model to produce it.
concepts: Power Fx is an Excel-like low-code formula language for manipulating data, parsing strings, and evaluating conditions in agent logic.
Prefix variables by scope, such as `Topic.`, `Global.`, `System.`, or `Environment.`, when you use them in formulas.
Copilot Studio formulas use US-style number formatting and commas as parameter separators.
steps: Create a topic and add a **Question** node.
For **Enter a message**, enter "What is your name?".
Under **Identify**, select the **Person name** entity.
Under **Save user response as**, select `Var1` and name it `customerName`.
Under the **Question** node, select **+**, and then select **Set a variable value**.
Under **Set variable**, select **Create new** and name it `capsName`.
In **To value**, select the **>** arrow, and then select **Formula**.
In **fx**, enter `Upper(Text(Topic.customerName))`, and then select **Insert**.
Under the **Question** node, select **+**, and then select **Send a message**.
Enter "HELLO ", select **{x}**, and then select `capsName`.
validation: The computed variable holds the exact expected value for at least three inputs.
Every condition branch has been exercised at least once.

features.name: SharePoint knowledge
features.harnessNote: SharePoint knowledge is also available on the Microsoft Copilot harness; see mc-knowledge for those steps.
features.summary: Ground the agent in SharePoint sites or lists so it answers from your organization's content.
features.whyItMatters: SharePoint is where many organizations already keep policies, procedures, and list-based operational data. Grounding there gives immediate, permission-trimmed value without moving that content into a separate repository.
concepts: SharePoint knowledge uses the signed-in user's Microsoft Entra ID permissions; content is returned only when the user can access it.
Register the specific site, folder, or list the agent should use; the agent searches the registered URL and subpaths, not sibling or parent locations.
Detailed names and descriptions help generative orchestration decide when to use the source.

In **Featured**, select **SharePoint**.
Enter the SharePoint URL, or select **Browse items** for lists; separate multiple URLs with **Shift** + **Enter** if needed.
Add a name and a detailed description for the source.
Select **Add to agent** to finish adding the knowledge source.
Ask a question that can only be answered from that source and check the citation and permission behavior.

features.whyItMatters: Escalation is the safety net of a contact-center agent. A defined path hands the customer to a human representative, with conversation context where the path supports it, instead of leaving the customer stuck.
concepts: **Escalate** is a prebuilt system tool with three paths: **Teams Phone** for immediate voice assistance, **Email** when a specialist can follow up later, and **Customer Engagement** for a live representative.

With **Customer Engagement**, a customer can ask for a live agent at any point, or the agent's instructions can trigger it. The agent sends the entire conversation to the engagement hub, which finds the best available live agent.
Select **Make this the default tool** to use a path when an agent or sub-agent has no escalation configured. Each sub-agent can have its own escalation path, such as a different queue.

Select the primary agent's card, or a sub-agent's card, to open its configuration panel.
In the **Tools** section, select **Add tool**, select the **System tools** tab, and then select **Escalate**.
Choose the escalation path to configure: **Teams Phone**, **Email**, or **Customer Engagement**.
Enter a name and description for the tool.
For **Teams Phone**, under **Route the call**, choose **External phone number or SIP URI** or **Teams call queue via Tags**. For **Email**, enter one or more addresses under **Recipients**.
To use this path when an agent or sub-agent has no escalation configured, select **Make this the default tool**.
Select **Add**.

On the **Preview** tab, asking for a representative triggers the escalation instead of the agent attempting the task.

features.name: Skills (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Add a Generative skill for flexible behavior and a Topic skill for deterministic logic from the Add skill dialog.
features.whyItMatters: Skills package reusable behaviors. A Generative skill lets the agent reason in the moment, while a Topic skill gives the predictable, repeatable logic that customer-facing scenarios often need.
concepts: A **Generative** skill is instructions-based: the agent reasons over your instructions. A **Topic** skill is a deterministic, authored flow of steps and conditions, the same concept as Topics elsewhere in Copilot Studio.
A generative skill name is kebab-case, up to 64 characters, with a description of up to 200 characters that the orchestrator uses to route requests.
To preserve conversation context, keep each skill to about 3,000 characters of instructions and use no more than 10 skills per sub-agent. These are recommendations, not hard limits.

features.name: Add a sub-agent (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Build a specialist sub-agent inside the primary agent, pass data with input and output variables, and test that routing reaches it.
features.whyItMatters: Sub-agents work like departments in a contact center. Each handles one focused intent with its own tools, knowledge, and escalation path, and the primary agent routes between them.
concepts: A sub-agent shares configuration, deployment, and application lifecycle management (ALM) with its primary agent. A connected agent keeps its own, can be reused across primary agents, and is covered in a separate module.

The primary agent's orchestration evaluates each message against the name, description, and instructions of every sub-agent. Keep sub-agents mutually exclusive and avoid similar names or descriptions.

A sub-agent has a **Name** of up to 42 characters, a **Description** of up to 1,024 characters, and **Instructions** of up to 20,000 characters. For output, choose whether the response is returned verbatim or summarized by the primary agent.

In the **Instructions** section, describe the sub-agent's role, tone, and rules.

features.name: Connect a Microsoft Foundry agent (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Prepare a Microsoft Foundry agent, add it as a connected agent from the Build tab, and publish the primary agent so it can communicate with Azure.
features.whyItMatters: A connected agent keeps its own configuration and lifecycle, so another team can own it and several primary agents can reuse it. Its model also affects response time, which matters on voice.
concepts: For this harness, a connected agent is currently an agent hosted in Microsoft Foundry. It can't reference tools, topics, events, sub-agents, or variables from the primary agent's orchestration.

The Foundry agent must have the **Activity protocol** endpoint enabled. A new Foundry agent exposes only the **Responses** and **A2A** endpoints by default, and without the Activity endpoint the connection fails at runtime with a 400 error.
The model selected in Microsoft Foundry affects how long the agent takes to answer, so choose one with latency that suits the scenario, especially for a voice channel.

features.name: Memory (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Turn Memory on for the agent, define custom parameters with Replace or Append, reference memory variables in instructions, and test continuity across conversations.
features.whyItMatters: A returning customer is met with continuity instead of a cold start, but remembered context can be incomplete or stale, so you need to know what it holds, how long it lasts, and how to use it safely.
concepts: Memory carries short-term conversation context for 30 days. Two built-in types are active when it is on: **Customer profile** (`/customerName`) and **Conversation history** (`/pastOpenIntentList` and `/pastConversationSummary`).

You can define up to five custom parameters with a unique name, a data type of string, number, or boolean, a description of 30 to 300 characters, and up to 10 allowed values of up to 30 characters each. **Replace** keeps the latest value, and **Append** keeps a timestamped list.

One agent-level control governs the root agent and all child agents, and turning it off does not delete stored context. Don't use remembered text as proof of identity or as an authoritative record, and verify it before consequential actions. Learn does not name where the control appears in the product.
steps: Open your agent in Copilot Studio.
Find the single agent-level control for Memory and turn it on, and confirm the change when prompted.

Optionally add a custom parameter. Give it a unique name, a data type, a description that tells the agent what to look for, and the allowed values, and then choose **Replace** or **Append** as its update mode.
In the agent's instructions, type / to reference the built-in variables, such as `/customerName` or `/pastConversationSummary`, where they should shape the response.
Have a test conversation that shares a detail, such as a customer name or an open request, and then start a new conversation.
Check whether the agent uses the remembered context, and confirm any important fact with the customer.
validation: Memory is on for the agent, and any custom parameter shows its data type, allowed values, and update mode.
A later conversation applies context captured in an earlier one, and a fact you changed is confirmed rather than trusted blindly.

features.name: Voice settings (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Open Voice Settings and tune the voice font, DTMF behavior, speech sensitivity or voice activity detection, silence detection, and latency messaging.
features.whyItMatters: Voice is not web chat with audio attached. How the agent sounds, when it decides a caller has finished speaking, and what it does during silence or delay decide whether a phone call feels natural.
concepts: Every agent supports Speech by default, and Voice is a configurable feature of it. Sub-agents inherit the voice settings of the primary agent.

With **Auto — optimized for cost**, speech uses Microsoft Neural Text-to-Speech with voice name, **Speaking speed**, and **Voice pitch**. With **Auto — optimized for latency**, you choose a built-in voice and a **Server VAD** or **Semantic VAD** mode.
Silence detection isn't on by default, so an agent waits indefinitely for a silent caller unless you turn it on and configure a reprompt. Latency messaging applies only to telephony channels.
steps: Open your agent in Copilot Studio and select the **Build** tab.
Select the primary agent's card to open its configuration panel.
Select **Voice Settings** to open the **Voice Settings** dialog.
On the voice font tab, review the **Primary language**, select a **Voice name**, and adjust **Speaking speed** and **Voice pitch**. Select **Try it out** to hear the voice.
In the DTMF settings, turn the **Allow DTMF** toggle on or off, and set the **Interdigit timeout (ms)** and **Termination key**.
Configure speech sensitivity: set **Sensitivity**, or for the latency mode choose **Server VAD** (**Threshold**, **Prefix padding**, **Silence duration**) or **Semantic VAD** (**Eagerness**).
Under **Silence detection timeout**, choose **No silence timeout** or **Silence detection timeout**, and then configure the **Silence Detection** event.
Under **Latency options**, choose **Play a message** or **Play an audio file**, and set the **Latency message**, **Send message delay (ms)**, and **Minimum playback time (ms)**.
Select **Save**, and then test with **Voice Call** on the **Preview** tab.
validation: The **Voice Settings** dialog shows the values you saved.
In a **Voice Call** test, the agent speaks with the chosen voice and re-prompts politely during silence instead of dropping the call.

features.name: Preview and test an agent (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Test the saved agent in Web Chat and Voice Call on the Preview tab, read the Activity map, and break the agent on purpose.
features.whyItMatters: An agent that looks correct on the Build tab can still fail in conversation, and voice has failure modes that text never shows. Testing before you publish catches routing, tool, knowledge, and guardrail problems.
concepts: The **Preview** tab has **Web Chat**, with a reasoning trace and a full transcript, and **Voice Call**, a live voice conversation with a **Live Transcript** panel. It runs your saved agent, not unsaved edits.

Test five layers in order: greeting and scope, routing, tools and topics, knowledge, and guardrails. The Activity map shows routing, tool calls, and topic execution, so you can tell a reasoning failure from a plumbing failure.
Start a new test session between scenarios because context carries over, and fix one thing at a time before you re-run.
steps: Save your changes on the **Build** tab, and then select the **Preview** tab.
Select **Web Chat** at the top of the **Preview** tab, and open the Activity map beside the chat.
Run the happy path first as a realistic customer with a complete goal, and verify every fact in the final recap against the transcript.
Then break it on purpose: skip a required detail, change your mind, ask something out of scope, trigger an escalation rule, and ask the agent to repeat an earlier detail.
Select **Voice Call**, grant microphone access, and speak a full request. Watch the **Live Transcript**, interrupt the agent mid-sentence, and stay silent for several seconds.
Start a new session, fix one issue, save, and re-run the same scenario and your other passing scenarios.
validation: The happy path completes end to end, and escalation and refusal rules fire reliably.
Voice responses are short, and a confirmation code is spelled out character by character.

instructions: Open the **Preview** tab and select **Web Chat**.

features.name: Authentication settings (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Set the orchestration-wide Authentication mode and turn on Voice authentication from the Security tab of Shared Settings, and review the grounding and file upload options on the Details tab.
features.whyItMatters: Shared Settings apply across every agent in the orchestration. Chat can sign users in but Speech cannot, so identity, grounding, and file handling need deliberate choices for both modalities.
concepts: The **Security** tab sets one **Authentication mode** for all agents in the orchestration (for example, **No authentication**) and, separately, **Voice authentication** for caller verification on voice channels.
Voice authentication needs an environment with Dynamics 365 apps enabled and uses biometric authentication, authentication policies, and one-time passcode challenge rules.

On the **Details** tab, **Allow ungrounded responses** lets the agent answer from general model knowledge, **Use information from the web** uses Grounding with Bing Search, which might send data outside your compliance boundary, and **File uploads** accepts files up to 15 MB that are processed per conversation and not stored.

features.name: Biometric Authentication for callers (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Enable Biometric Authentication under Voice capabilities, choose how to identify the caller, set the lookup table, and require verification before the agent runs another tool.
features.whyItMatters: Callers cannot sign in on a Speech channel, so the agent must verify identity another way before it discusses account details or runs sensitive tools.
concepts: An admin first enables biometric authentication and fraud detection in the Microsoft Contact Center Intelligence portal, which pre-enables the **Biometric authentication** setting for every agent.

**Identify user** uses **Use phone number** or **Use custom identifier**, and the lookup table defaults to the Dataverse **Contact** or **Account** tables. Name the tool for a specific purpose, because a generic name can make the orchestrator over-invoke it.
Switching to **Advanced editing** is a one-way change. To gate another tool, add a **Condition** node that checks the Voice Authentication status variable for "Verified" before the tool runs.
steps: Ask an admin to enable biometric authentication and fraud detection in the Microsoft Contact Center Intelligence portal, and confirm the **Biometric authentication** setting under **Shared Settings** > **Security**.
In the **Voice capabilities** section of the **Build** tab, select the primary agent's card (or a sub-agent's card), and select **Enable** next to **Biometric Authentication**.
Give the tool a specific name and description, such as one that verifies callers before discussing account details.
Under **Identify user**, select **Use phone number** or **Use custom identifier**.
Turn on **Use selected identifiers to look up user record**, and set the **Lookup table**, for example the **Contact** table.
Under **Authenticate user**, review the **Authentication profile** and the resolved **Unique identifier**.
Select **Add behavior** to save the tool.
To protect another tool, use **Advanced editing**, add a **Condition** node on the Voice Authentication status variable, and place the tool in the branch for a verified caller.

features.name: Export and import an agent (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Move an agent between environments with an unmanaged solution, and know what does not transfer.
features.whyItMatters: Some channels, such as certain contact center connections and voice authentication, need an environment with Dynamics 365 apps enabled. Solutions are how you move or promote an agent safely.
concepts: Export and import use the same solutions-based procedure as the standard harness. You can't export managed solutions, and you need at least the System Customizer security role.
Not all components and properties transfer: for example conversation ID, environment ID, and topic-level or node-level comments don't, and the agent icon and channel details might be empty.

You must deploy the imported agent before it can be shared, and you must configure user authentication for it again. Add any flows, custom connectors, or environment variables the agent uses to the solution too.
steps: Open the solution explorer in Copilot Studio.
Create a new solution, or select an existing unmanaged solution.
Select **Add existing** > **Agent** > **Agent**, select the agent, and then select **Add**. Add any flows, custom connectors, or environment variables the agent uses.
Select the unmanaged solution, select **Export solution**, and follow the Power Apps export experience.
In the target environment, open the solution explorer and select **Import solution**.
After the import finishes, select the imported solution, select **Agents**, and select the agent's name to open it.
Configure user authentication again, and then deploy the agent from the **Deploy** tab.
validation: The imported agent opens in the target environment with its instructions, tools, and knowledge intact.
User authentication is reconfigured and the agent is deployed before it is shared.

features.name: Copilot Credits and cost controls (Customer Conversation harness)
features.summary: Find the Copilot Credits a Customer Conversation agent consumes on the Monitor tab and review the admin controls that allocate, limit, and track them.
features.whyItMatters: Customer conversations consume credits based on complexity and modality, and Voice Biometrics adds more. Planning capacity and limits early prevents an agent from stopping when credits run out or consuming more than expected.
concepts: Copilot Credit use varies by conversation complexity and modality: digital, GenAI voice, and premium voice. Using, building, testing, and evaluating agents might consume credits, and a Microsoft 365 Copilot license does not cover this usage.
Each voice enrollment or authentication interaction with Voice Biometrics consumes 6 credits, so a voice conversation with two biometric interactions consumes 12 additional credits.

Admins control spend with environment allocations, turning off **Draw from the available capacity in my tenant**, and agent-level monthly limits with **Stop usage**. Azure budgets and alerts for pay-as-you-go send notifications but do not stop consumption.
steps: Open the agent's **Monitor** tab and review the **Billing** panel for the Copilot Credits billed in the selected period. Select **See billing** for more detail.
Use the Copilot Credits estimator linked from **Overview of usage-based billing** to model light, medium, and heavy conversations by modality.
As an admin, sign in to the Power Platform admin center, select **Licensing**, and under **Products** select **Copilot Studio**.

Select **Manage Copilot Credits**, select the environment, enter the number of credits to allocate, and under **Capacity overages** clear **Draw from the available capacity in my tenant** if the environment should not use tenant capacity. Select **Save**.

Select **Manage Agents**, select the customer conversation agent, and select **Set limit**. Enter the monthly limit, configure the notification threshold, turn on **Stop usage** if needed, and select **Save**.
Review consumption by tenant, environment, and agent, and compare it with expected conversation volume.
validation: You can show the credits billed for the agent on the **Monitor** tab.
You can name the controls that allocate and limit spend and where to review consumption.
